summary: Specifies PIM Light and the PIM Light Interface. Such an interface does not need a PIM Hello message to accept Join/Prune messages, and can signal multicast state over networks that cannot support full neighbor discovery, such as BIER networks connecting PIM domains.

eli5.summary: Normally routers must say hello before swapping group-delivery requests. PIM Light lets them skip the hello where it cannot work.

subtitle: A PIM interface type that accepts Join/Prune messages without a Hello, for networks where PIM neighbor discovery does not fit.

tldr.problem: Normal PIM routers discard Join/Prune messages from a router they have not seen a Hello from, which blocks multicast signaling over networks such as BIER that cannot support full PIM neighborship.
tldr.mechanism: A PIM Light Interface (PLI) accepts Join/Prune messages from an unknown router without a Hello, supports only a limited set of PIM message types, and leaves things like DR election to the surrounding network design.
tldr.outcome: Multicast state can be signaled across a BIER network joining PIM domains, at the cost of neighbor discovery, DR election and Assert, so operators must prevent duplicate streams themselves.

today: RFC 9739 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: What PIM Light Is
sections.content:
This RFC defines PIM Light and the PIM Light Interface (PLI), a new type of PIM interface that allows signaling of PIM Join/Prune packets without full PIM neighbor discovery. It is useful where multicast state must be signaled over networks or media that cannot support full PIM neighborship, or where it is not desired. Such networks are called PIM Light domains.

PIM Light only supports PIM Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), including Source-Specific Multicast (PIM-SSM), as defined in RFC 7761.
sections.eli5: Routers usually introduce themselves before passing notes about which shows they want to watch. PIM Light is a way to pass the notes without the introduction.

sections.title: Why Skip the Hello
sections.content:
In RFC 7761, a router that gets a Join/Prune from an address it has not seen a PIM Hello from SHOULD discard that message. In some cases it is desirable to establish multicast state between two routers without forming a PIM neighborship, for example to signal state upstream between PIM domains over a network not optimized for PIM. The RFC's example is a Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER, RFC 8279) network connecting several PIM domains, where Join/Prune messages are tunneled over BIER.

A PLI accepts Join/Prune messages from an unknown router. Without Hellos there is no discovery of neighbors or their capabilities and no Designated Router (DR) election. The PIM Light router keeps no general-purpose state for neighbors and only processes Join/Prune messages from downstream routers into its multicast routing table.

Because of these limits, a PLI should be used only in very specific scenarios where PIM-SM is not suitable, and the deployment MUST ensure there is no multicast packet duplication, such as several upstream routers sending the same stream to one downstream router.
sections.eli5: Skipping the introduction means you do not know who your neighbors are, so whoever builds the network has to make sure two neighbors do not both send you the same thing.

sections.title: Supported Message Types
sections.content:
PIM Light supports only these message types from the IANA PIM Message Types registry, plus any future PIM message types whose destination is a unicast IP address. Other message types MUST NOT be processed if received on a PLI.

  • type 1 (Register)
  • type 2 (Register Stop)
  • type 3 (Join/Prune)
  • type 8 (Candidate RP Advertisement)
  • type 13.0 (PIM Packed Null-Register)
  • type 13.1 (PIM Packed Register-Stop)

PIM Dense Mode (RFC 3973) and Bidirectional PIM (RFC 5015) are not supported.
sections.eli5: PIM Light only understands a short list of message kinds. If something else shows up, it ignores it.

sections.title: What Goes Missing Without Hellos
sections.content:
Join Attribute. A PLI does not use the Hello option for Join Attributes (RFC 5384), so it SHOULD NOT send a Join containing a Join Attribute. It can do so when neighbors are known by configuration to handle the attribute, or when other documents allow certain attributes without configuration.

DR election. It is not supported on a PIM Light router. The network design must ensure DR election occurs within the PIM domain. If redundant PIM routers sit at the edge of a BIER domain, they MUST establish PIM adjacency per RFC 7761 to prevent duplication and to elect a DR, and only the DR forwards the Join or Prune over the BIER tunnel.

PIM Assert. RFC 7761 says Assert should only be accepted from a known neighbor. In PIM Light, care must be taken to avoid duplicate streams from several upstream PIM Light routers. In a BIER example, a downstream IBBR can find the nearest EBBRs to the source using SPF with post-processing and choose one by a rule such as lowest or highest IP address, moving to the next if the chosen one goes offline. That selection algorithm is beyond the scope of the RFC.
sections.eli5: Without introductions, there is no way to vote on who is in charge or to settle arguments about who sends the stream. So the people who design the network must arrange that in advance.

sections.title: Configuring and Protecting a PLI
sections.content:
Because neighbor adjacency is not checked, there must be a way to enable a PLI on an interface. Join/Prune messages not received from a PIM neighbor MUST be dropped unless a PLI is enabled on the interface. A PLI may be enabled automatically by an underlying mechanism on a logical interface, such as one connecting BIER edge routers.

Failures in the PIM Light domain may go undiscovered, so routes are not pruned toward the source and upstream routers keep sending until the outgoing interface (OIF) expires. Other implementation-specific protocols can detect failure. One example is Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD): if BFD to the far-end PLI goes down, the upstream router must remove that PLI from its OIF list for the (S,G) route. In the BIER example, the Upstream BIER Edge Router can prune (S,G) toward the source when the Downstream BIER Edge Router becomes unreachable.
sections.eli5: You have to switch the feature on by hand for each link. And since nobody says hello, you need some other way, like a heartbeat check, to notice when the other side has gone away.

sections.title: Reliable Transport for PIM Light
sections.content:
RFC 6559 defines PIM Over Reliable Transport (PORT), carrying Join/Prune messages over TCP or SCTP, both using destination port number 8471. Normally the Hello carries a Connection ID, an IPv4 or IPv6 address used to set up the connection. With TCP, it decides which peer opens actively and which passively. With SCTP it is not used for this, since SCTP can handle call collision (see RFC 9260).

PIM Light has no Hellos, so the PLI can be configured with the Connection ID. For PIM Light over TCP, each end must be explicitly and correctly configured as either active or passive open to avoid call collision.
sections.eli5: If the notes are sent over a reliable pipe, someone has to decide who starts the call. With no introductions, you set that up by hand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Since adjacency is not verified, implementations must ensure that only Join/Prune messages arriving at a configured PLI are processed. Join/Prune messages on an interface not configured as a PLI MUST be discarded. As a secondary defense, route policies SHOULD process only Join/Prune messages for the desired (S,G) pairs, and all other (S,G) pairs MUST be discarded.

The security considerations of RFC 7761 and RFC 4607 SHOULD be considered where appropriate. Only forged Join/Prune messages are a potential attack vector, since PIM Light does not process Hello or Assert messages. The authentication mechanisms in RFC 5796 can be applied via IPsec ESP or, optionally, AH. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Because anyone could slip in a note, the router only reads notes that come in through doors you opened on purpose, and only for the shows you approved.
